concepts.def: A test in which a sample of a compound is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame; some metal ions give the flame a distinctive colour, and that colour identifies the metal ion.
A positively charged ion. The metal ions identified by flame tests and by sodium hydroxide solution are cations.
The flame colour produced by lithium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by sodium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by potassium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by calcium compounds in a flame test.
The flame colour produced by copper compounds in a flame test.
When a sample contains a mixture of ions, one strong flame colour can hide, or mask, the colour produced by another metal ion, so that ion is not seen.

concepts.term: Identifying a species from test results
concepts.def: Combining the results of the flame test, the sodium hydroxide test, the carbonate test, the halide test and the sulfate test to name the metal ion and the negative ion, and so the compound.
Adding sodium hydroxide solution to a solution of an unknown salt; the colour of the metal hydroxide precipitate that forms identifies the metal ion.
An insoluble solid formed when two solutions are mixed. In these tests the precipitate is a metal hydroxide, a silver halide or barium sulfate.
Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions all form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.
Of the three white hydroxide precipitates, only aluminium hydroxide dissolves when excess sodium hydroxide solution is added; this distinguishes aluminium ions from calcium and magnesium ions.
Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured, not white, precipitates with sodium hydroxide solution.
The blue precipitate formed when sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution containing copper(II) ions.
Iron(II) ions give a green precipitate and iron(III) ions give a brown precipitate with sodium hydroxide solution.
A balanced symbol equation showing a metal salt solution reacting with sodium hydroxide solution to give the insoluble metal hydroxide, for example MgCl2 + 2NaOH -> Mg(OH)2 + 2NaCl.
Adding a dilute acid to the substance; carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas, seen as fizzing.
Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater: the gas is bubbled through limewater, which turns cloudy.
Adding dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution to the solution; halide ions produce a silver halide precipitate.
Silver chloride is white, silver bromide is cream and silver iodide is yellow.
Adding dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution; sulfate ions produce a white precipitate of barium sulfate.
Using chemical tests to identify the ions in unknown single ionic compounds, covering the ions from the flame tests section through to the sulfates section.
A method of detecting and identifying elements and compounds using a machine rather than a chemical test. Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.
Compared with the chemical tests in this specification, instrumental methods are more accurate, more sensitive (they detect very small amounts) and faster.
An instrumental method used to analyse metal ions in solutions.
In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame and the light given out is passed through a spectroscope; the output is a line spectrum.
A set of results for known substances, in the same chart or tabular form as the sample result, against which an instrumental result is compared to identify the ions present.

mcqs.q: A student holds a small sample of an unknown ionic compound on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame, and a strong colour appears. What does the flame colour identify?
options: the metal ion, the cation, present in that compound
the negative ion, the anion, in the compound
the compound as a whole and not one of its ions
the temperature reached by the Bunsen flame
mcqs.explain: Flame tests can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

mcqs.q: Lithium chloride is held on a clean wire in a hot Bunsen flame. What is seen?
options: The flame turns a bright yellow colour.
The flame turns a deep crimson colour.
The flame turns an orange-red colour.
The flame turns a pale lilac colour.
mcqs.explain: Lithium compounds result in a crimson flame.

mcqs.q: Sodium chloride is used in a flame test. Which statement describes the result?
options: Sodium ions colour the flame bright orange.
Sodium ions colour the flame orange-red.
Sodium ions colour the flame yellow.
Sodium ions colour the flame lilac.
mcqs.explain: Sodium compounds result in a yellow flame.

mcqs.q: Potassium bromide is tested in a flame test. What is the result?
options: The flame colour produced is yellow.
The flame colour produced is crimson.
The flame colour produced is orange-red.
The flame colour produced is lilac.
mcqs.explain: Potassium compounds result in a lilac flame.

mcqs.q: Calcium nitrate gives a distinctive colour in a flame test. Which colour is it?
options: a pale green flame colour
an orange-red flame colour
a bright crimson colour
a bright yellow colour
mcqs.explain: Calcium compounds result in an orange-red flame.

mcqs.q: Copper(II) sulfate is held in a hot Bunsen flame during a flame test. What is seen?
options: The flame is coloured a crimson red.
The flame is coloured pale blue.
The flame is coloured a bright green.
The flame colour does not change at all.
mcqs.explain: Copper compounds result in a green flame.

mcqs.q: A solution contains both sodium ions and potassium ions. In a flame test only a yellow colour is seen. Why is the lilac colour of potassium not seen?
options: The potassium ions are destroyed in the flame.
The two colours mix to give a new colour.
Potassium needs a hotter flame than this one.
The intense sodium colour masks the lilac.
mcqs.explain: If a sample containing a mixture of ions is used some flame colours can be masked.

mcqs.q: An unknown compound gives a yellow flame test colour. Its solution gives a white precipitate when dilute hydrochloric acid and then barium chloride solution are added. What is the compound?
options: sodium sulfate
potassium sulfate
sodium carbonate
sodium chloride
mcqs.explain: The yellow flame shows sodium ions and the white precipitate with acidified barium chloride shows sulfate ions.

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to a solution of an unknown salt and a precipitate forms. Which ion in the salt does this test identify?
options: the negative ion in the salt, its anion
the hydroxide ion from the sodium hydroxide
the positive metal ion in the salt, its cation
both of the ions in the salt at one time
mcqs.explain: Sodium hydroxide solution can be used to identify some metal ions (cations).

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added, a few drops at a time, to separate solutions of aluminium ions, calcium ions and magnesium ions. What is seen in each tube?
options: A white precipitate forms in two of the tubes.
A coloured precipitate forms in each tube.
A white precipitate forms in one tube only.
A white precipitate forms in all three tubes.
mcqs.explain: Solutions of aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions form white precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.

mcqs.q: Excess sodium hydroxide solution is now added to the three white precipitates formed from aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions. What happens?
options: Only the aluminium hydroxide dissolves.
Only the calcium hydroxide dissolves.
All three of the white hydroxides dissolve.
None of the three precipitates dissolves.
mcqs.explain: Only the aluminium hydroxide precipitate dissolves in excess sodium hydroxide solution.

mcqs.q: Which set of metal ions all give coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added to their solutions?
options: aluminium, calcium and magnesium ions
copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III)
copper(II), calcium and magnesium ions
aluminium, calcium and the iron(III) ion.
mcqs.explain: Solutions of copper(II), iron(II) and iron(III) ions form coloured precipitates when sodium hydroxide solution is added.

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution. What is seen?
options: a green precipitate forms
a blue precipitate forms
a white precipitate is formed
a brown precipitate is seen
mcqs.explain: Iron(III) forms a brown precipitate.

mcqs.q: A solution gives a green precipitate when sodium hydroxide solution is added. Which ion does the solution contain?
options: The solution contains iron(II) ions.
The solution contains copper(II) ions.
It is a solution of iron(III) ions.
It is a magnesium salt in water.
mcqs.explain: Iron(II) forms a green precipitate.

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to copper(II) sulfate solution and a blue precipitate forms. Which equation for this reaction is correct and balanced?
options: CuSO4 + NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> Cu(OH)2 + Na2SO4
2CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> 2Cu(OH)2 + 2Na2SO4
CuSO4 + 2NaOH -> CuOH + Na2SO4 + H2
mcqs.explain: Two hydroxide ions are needed for each Cu2+ ion, and every atom balances.

mcqs.q: Iron(II) sulfate solution reacts with sodium hydroxide solution to give a green precipitate. Which equation is correct and balanced?
options: Fe2SO4 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + Na2SO4
FeSO4 + NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4
FeSO4 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + Na2SO4 + H2
mcqs.explain: Iron(II) is Fe2+, so the insoluble hydroxide is Fe(OH)2 and two NaOH are needed.

mcqs.q: Dilute hydrochloric acid is added to a white solid that is thought to be a carbonate. What is seen, and what gas is given off?
options: It fizzes, giving off carbon dioxide gas.
It fizzes, giving off hydrogen gas.
It fizzes, giving off oxygen gas.
It dissolves quietly, giving off no gas.
mcqs.explain: Carbonates react with dilute acids to form carbon dioxide gas.

mcqs.q: The gas given off when a carbonate reacts with a dilute acid is bubbled through limewater. What is the positive result?
options: The limewater relights a glowing splint.
The limewater turns cloudy, or milky.
The limewater turns a bright blue.
The limewater becomes colourless.
mcqs.explain: Carbon dioxide can be identified with limewater, which turns cloudy.

mcqs.q: Dilute nitric acid and then silver nitrate solution are added to a solution of an unknown halide. A cream precipitate forms. What does the solution contain?
options: The unknown solution contains chloride ions.
The unknown solution contains carbonate ions.
The unknown solution contains bromide ions.
The unknown solution contains iodide ions.
mcqs.explain: Silver bromide is cream.

mcqs.q: A solution is acidified with dilute nitric acid and silver nitrate solution is added. A yellow precipitate forms. Which ion is present?
options: the bromide ion, Br-
the chloride ion, Cl-
the sulfate ion, SO4 2-
the iodide ion, I-
mcqs.explain: Silver iodide is yellow.

mcqs.q: A student wants to show that a solution contains sulfate ions. What should be added, and what is a positive result?
options: dilute nitric acid, then silver nitrate solution: a white precipitate
dilute hydrochloric acid, then barium chloride solution: a white precipitate
dilute hydrochloric acid, then sodium hydroxide: a white precipitate
barium chloride solution alone: a cream coloured precipitate
mcqs.explain: Sulfate ions in solution produce a white precipitate with barium chloride solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid.

mcqs.q: Barium chloride solution is added to a solution in the presence of dilute hydrochloric acid, and a white precipitate forms. What does this show?
options: Chloride ions are present in this solution.
Carbonate ions are present in solution.
Sulfate ions are present in the solution.
Barium ions are present in solution.
mcqs.explain: The white precipitate is barium sulfate, so sulfate ions are present.

mcqs.q: In Required practical 7 a student is given a solution of a single unknown ionic compound and must name it. Which plan will identify the compound?
options: adding sodium hydroxide, then more of it
adding barium chloride to test for chloride
just a flame test on its own is enough
a flame test, then a test for the anion
mcqs.explain: The compound is named only when both its metal ion and its negative ion have been identified.

mcqs.q: The specification describes instrumental methods of analysis. Which three words does it use?
options: accurate, sensitive and rapid
accurate and sensitive, but slow
cheap, simple and easy to carry
accurate, but far too slow to use.
mcqs.explain: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

mcqs.q: Give one advantage of using an instrumental method instead of the chemical tests in this specification.
options: It can be used without taking a sample at all.
It gives a result that never needs any checking.
It can detect a very small amount of a substance quickly.
It is always cheaper than a simple chemical test.
mcqs.explain: Instrumental methods are accurate, sensitive and rapid.

mcqs.q: Flame emission spectroscopy is an instrumental method. What is it used to analyse?
options: the non-metal ions present in solids
the non-metal ions dissolved in a solution
the mass of a solid sample taken
the metal ions present in solutions
mcqs.explain: Flame emission spectroscopy is used to analyse metal ions in solutions.

mcqs.q: In flame emission spectroscopy the sample is put into a flame. What happens to the light given out, and what is the output?
options: It passes into a spectroscope, giving a line spectrum.
It is split by a coloured filter into one colour.
It passes through a coloured filter, giving one colour.
It warms a sensor, giving a temperature reading.
mcqs.explain: The light given out is passed through a spectroscope and the output is a line spectrum.

mcqs.q: A student is given the line spectrum of a solution together with a reference set of line spectra for known metal ions. The sample spectrum contains every line of the lithium reference and every line of the calcium reference. What should the student conclude?
options: Only the ion with the brighter lines is present.
Lithium ions and calcium ions are both present.
Only the ion with the most intense lines is present.
Nothing can be concluded from a spectrum like this.
mcqs.explain: Each set of reference lines that appears in the sample spectrum shows that metal ion is present.

mcqs.q: Sodium hydroxide solution is added to iron(III) chloride solution and a brown precipitate forms. Which equation is correct and balanced?
options: FeCl3 + 2NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + 2NaCl
FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + 3NaCl
FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)3 + NaCl3
FeCl3 + 3NaOH -> Fe(OH)2 + 3NaCl
mcqs.explain: Fe3+ needs three hydroxide ions, and the three chloride ions give 3NaCl.

mcqs.q: A solution is analysed by flame emission spectroscopy. Sample lines (nm): 589, 671. Reference lines (nm): sodium 589; lithium 671; potassium 766; calcium 622. Which metal ions does the sample contain?
options: lithium and sodium ions
sodium ions on their own
sodium and potassium ions
potassium and calcium ions
mcqs.explain: Both reference lines, 589 nm and 671 nm, appear in the sample.
